passage_text:
Researchers investigated the effect of varying doses of a novel cognitive enhancer on reaction time in healthy adults. A randomized controlled trial enrolled 120 participants, who were assigned to one of four groups: placebo, low dose (10 mg), medium dose (20 mg), and high dose (30 mg). After a single dose, participants completed a computerized visual reaction time task. Table 1 summarizes the key findings.

Table 1. Reaction time outcomes by treatment group

| Treatment | Avg. Response Time (s) | SD | N |
|-----------|------------------------|----|---|
| Placebo   | 0.85                   | 0.10 | 30 |
| Low Dose  | 0.78                   | 0.12 | 30 |
| Medium Dose | 0.72                 | 0.11 | 30 |
| High Dose | 0.70                   | 0.15 | 30 |

The data suggest a dose‑response relationship, with higher doses associated with faster reaction times. Table 1 reports group means and SDs only; no significance tests are reported.

stem: Which treatment group had the lowest average response time according to Table 1?
explanation: The High Dose group has the lowest mean response time (0.70 s) versus 0.72 (medium), 0.78 (low) and 0.85 (placebo).
trap: Choosing Low Dose or Placebo by misreading which column is fastest; lower response time means faster.

stem: Which experimental design best controls for potential confounding variables in this study?
explanation: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) randomly assigns participants to treatment groups, thereby balancing known and unknown confounders across groups. This design is the gold standard for establishing causal relationships.
trap: Students may incorrectly think an observational study can control for confounders if it uses statistical adjustments.

stem: Calculate the pooled standard deviation for the Low Dose and High Dose groups. (Use n = 30 for each group.)
explanation: With equal n, pooled SD = sqrt((0.12^2 + 0.15^2)/2) = sqrt(0.01845) = 0.136 s, about 0.14 s.
trap: Picking one group's SD (0.12 or 0.15) or adding the SDs (0.27) instead of pooling variances.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?

options.A: The high-dose group had a faster mean response time than the low-dose group.
options.B: The placebo group had the fastest mean response time.
options.C: All four groups had the same number of participants.
options.D: The high-dose group had the largest SD.

explanation: Correct: The placebo group had the slowest mean response time (0.85 s), so B is not supported. Why the others are wrong: A) high dose 0.70 s versus low dose 0.78 s, so it is supported. C) every group has N = 30, so it is supported. D) the high-dose SD is 0.15, the largest listed, so it is supported.
trap: Focusing on the placebo column and assuming the reference group performed best, when its 0.85 s is the slowest mean.

stem: Which dose step produced the smallest additional reduction in mean response time?

options.D: All three steps gave equal reductions

explanation: Correct: The mean falls 0.07 s (0.85 to 0.78), 0.06 s (0.78 to 0.72) and 0.02 s (0.72 to 0.70), so the 20 to 30 mg step adds the least. Why the others are wrong: A) placebo to 10 mg gave the largest step (0.07 s). B) 10 to 20 mg gave 0.06 s. D) the three steps are not equal.
trap: Assuming each equal dose increase gives an equal gain in speed, when the step from 20 mg to 30 mg is much smaller than earlier steps.
